newsitem.title: USA: Diesel seen as promising for next-generation car.
newsitem.headline: Diesel seen as promising for next-generation car.

text.p: A lightweight diesel engine is the most promising power source for creating a cheap car capable of getting 80 miles per gallon by the year 2004, according to a report issued Thursday.

However, the head of a government-industry partnership to develop a car engine with greater fuel efficiency said the group will be unable to meet its goal without additional funding and a narrower focus.

The National Research Council report said none of the engines or fuel cells being considered for a hybrid car -- using both electric and conventional motors -- were affordable enough to meet the goals of the Partnership for a New Generation of Vehicles (PNGV).

But it said diesel was the most highly developed technology and most likely to be selected for the initial test vehicles. For this reason, more resources should be put into developing lightweight diesel engines.
President Clinton set up the PNGV in 1993, with the government and the Big Three automakers as a group each putting in about $300 million a year.
Committee Chairman Trevor Jones, chairman of the auto component company Echlin Inc., said more funding and better focusing of research were needed for the PNGV to meet its goals.

"Unless more resources are provided to speed up development and more attention is focused on technologies that show the most promise, PNGV will not succeed in producing an affordable, highly fuel-efficient production prototype vehicle by 2004," he said.
The committee, however, did not say how much additional money was needed from the government or Chrysler Corp., Ford Motor Co. and General Motors Corp.

The PNGV's aim is to build concept test vehicles by the year 2000 and production prototypes by 2004. The fuel economy of 80 miles per gallon would be three times greater than today's cars on average, while still meeting or exceeding current emission standards.
In its report, the committee noted that a major PNGV milestone was due at the end of this year when it was to select the most promising technologies for its concept cars.
The panel said that for the PNGV to meet its goals, programme managers should assess the progress of current technological research in the areas that include energy conversion and energy storage.
It said that with additional funding and better focused research, "it may be possible to produce a suitable diesel engine within the program's current schedule."

But the panel said that cutting diesel emissions remained a priority, especially since standards may be more restrictive by 2004. It said diesel research in Europe and Japan should be assessed to see if it can be applied to the PNGV programme.
Cost-effective fuel cells and gas turbine engines, also being considered as power sources, are unlikely to be developed in time to meet PNGV goals.

To meet the stringent PNGV fuel economy standards, it said, vehicles will most likely use batteries that store and recapture otherwise wasted energy, and more research should be put into developing these.

Looking at long term prospects, the commmitee said while the PNGV should concentrate on meeting its programme objectives, it should also fund other technologies that may be successful later, such as fuel cells and or gas turbines.
